questions.question: What are the primitive types in JavaScript, and how does copying a primitive differ from copying an object?
questions.answer: The seven primitives are string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, and bigint. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. Primitives are copied by value, so changing the copy leaves the original alone. Objects are copied by reference, so two names can point at the same object and a mutation through one is visible through the other. `typeof []` is `"object"` and `typeof null` is also `"object"`, so use `Array.isArray` and `=== null` instead.
key_points: Primitives copy by value, objects by reference

questions.question: Explain the difference between `null` and `undefined`, including how each behaves in `typeof`, `==`, and `JSON.stringify`.
questions.answer: `undefined` means a value was never assigned — an uninitialized variable, a missing argument, or a missing property. `null` is an intentional empty value that you assign. `typeof undefined` is `"undefined"`; `typeof null` is `"object"` because of a historic bug. `null == undefined` is true but `null === undefined` is false. In JSON, `JSON.stringify` drops properties whose value is `undefined` but keeps `null`.

questions.question: Predict the output: `console.log([1] + 1); console.log([1] - 1);`
questions.answer: It prints `"11"` then `0`. The `+` operator sees an object and a number; the array becomes the string `"1"`, so the result is string concatenation. The `-` operator has no string meaning, so both sides convert to numbers: `Number([1])` is `1`, and `1 - 1` is `0`.
key_points: Array to primitive goes through toString
Same value, different operators, different types

questions.question: Why is `Boolean([])` true while `[] == false` is also true?
questions.answer: They use different algorithms. `Boolean([])` checks object identity: every object is truthy, including an empty array. Loose equality converts the array to a primitive (`""`) and then compares `"" == false`, which converts both to numbers (`0 == 0`) and yields true. Truthiness is not the same rule as `==` coercion.

questions.question: List the falsy values and explain the difference between `isNaN` and `Number.isNaN`.
questions.answer: The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `" "`, `[]`, and `{}`. The global `isNaN(x)` first coerces `x` to a number, so `isNaN("abc")` is true. `Number.isNaN(x)` does not coerce, so it is true only when the value is actually the number `NaN`; `Number.isNaN("abc")` is false.
